content.p: On 9 December 1947, Dutch colonial soldiers entered a village in West Java and shot the men and boys who lived there. The village was Rawagede, and the killings are called the Rawagede massacre. For more than sixty years no soldier was prosecuted and the Dutch state did not formally apologise. The story changed in 2011, when a court in The Hague held the state responsible and the government then apologised to the families. The death toll is still disputed, and so is the number of people who received money.

Rawagede was a village in West Java, in what was then the Dutch East Indies. Indonesia declared its independence in 1945, and the Netherlands tried to keep control of its former colony through military action. Indonesian fighters and Dutch troops were locked in what sources call the 1945-49 Indonesian War for Independence. DutchNews reports that Indonesia was granted sovereignty in 1949, after the armed struggle.

In 1947 the Netherlands ran a major military campaign against the independence movement. DW describes the Rawagede killings as part of that campaign, which it names Operatie Product. DW reports that the forces had been sent to intervene against massacres of Dutch, Eurasian and Chinese people by Indonesian fighters and the Bersiap militia. Al Jazeera reported that the Dutch troops came to the village to find an independence fighter.

According to the Associated Press, Dutch troops arrived in Rawagede on 9 December 1947 and demanded that residents tell them where Lukas Kustaryo could be found. The villagers said they did not know. The men were then lined up and shot. UCA News reports that 300 Dutch troops led by Major Alphons Wijnen moved into the village. The sources describe Kustaryo differently. AP calls him a local soldier. UCA News calls him the commander of the Siliwangi Division, which had often given the Dutch troops problems.

Al Jazeera reported that the troops killed men and boys while their families and neighbours watched. AP reports that only a few escaped, and that at least one man was shot and wounded as he ran. Survivors described the aftermath. Al Jazeera quotes a survivor, Cawi: "There were dead bodies everywhere, many of which we found in the river after the shooting stopped." AP reports that the women of the village, together with the few older men who remained, buried the dead the next day in shallow graves, digging with their bare hands.

The number of men killed is the most contested point in the whole case. Dutch officials say 150 people were killed. A 1969 Dutch investigation, as JURIST reports it, also put the figure at 150. A support group and the local community say 431 men and boys died, and DW says 431 is the figure in most estimates. AP gives a range of 150 to 430 for the men who died. The Jakarta Post describes the Dutch troops as having killed more than 400 people.

The Dutch government accepted in 1995 that summary executions had taken place, yet its official papers still give 150. The victims' side and the local community give 431. DutchNews repeats the two figures side by side.

The UN investigative commission of 1948 condemned the killings. According to AP and the Dutch press release, the commission called the acts "deliberate and ruthless". DW quotes the same report as calling them "deliberate and merciless". No soldier was ever prosecuted for Rawagede, according to AP.

In 1968 a Dutch report acknowledged "violent excesses" in Indonesia. It described the fighting as a "police action" that Dutch troops had carried out in response to guerrilla warfare and terror attacks, according to AP. A television documentary later revisited the bloodbath. In 1995 the government conceded that summary executions had taken place in Rawagede, but said prosecutions were no longer possible. In 2005 former Foreign Minister Ben Bot expressed deep regret for offences by Dutch forces in Indonesia in 1947, according to AP. None of these steps included an apology to the families or compensation.

Ten survivors formally held the Netherlands responsible in 2008, and in December 2009 they decided to sue the Dutch state, according to DW. DutchNews reports that the attorney general had turned the claim away in 2008 as out of time. JURIST describes a 2008 Dutch court ruling in the government's favour on the statute of limitations. The lawyer for the plaintiffs was Liesbeth Zegveld.

The Hague District Court ruled on Wednesday 14 September 2011. DutchNews reports that the court found the Dutch state liable for the damages. The court said the state could not rely on the statute of limitations, because the case concerned people who were direct victims of war crimes committed by Dutch soldiers. AP quotes the written judgment, which said the Netherlands had "acted illegally" against the plaintiffs "through the execution of their then-husbands", and that the state was liable to compensate them for "past and future suffering." The normal limit is five years, the court said, but it made an exception because of the seriousness of the offences.

Zegveld said, "Justice has been done," according to Al Jazeera. She added that the state could not "just sit in silence for 60 years waiting for the case to go away of the plaintiffs to die and then appeal to the statute of limitations." The state's lawyer, Bert-Jan Houtzagers, was taken aback by the decision and said he would read the 17-page judgment before deciding on an appeal, AP reports.

A press release dated 5 December 2011, issued by the relatives' lawyer, said the state had reached a settlement with nine surviving relatives. It said the state would pay damages and offer its apologies for the executions of 9 December 1947. Zegveld said the state was not appealing the verdict, and she called that and the apology "very much appreciated by the surviving relatives." Foreign Minister Uri Rosenthal said the apology "does justice to the seriousness of events in Rawagede", according to DutchNews.

On 9 December 2011, the sixty-fourth anniversary of the killings, Dutch ambassador Tjeerd de Zwaan spoke at a memorial in Balongsari. Al Jazeera quotes him: "In this context and on behalf of the Dutch government, I apologise for the tragedy that took place in Rawagede on the 9th of December, 1947." He repeated the apology in Indonesian to applause. Some of the people in the crowd wept, and Al Jazeera reports that the ambassador said the massacre showed how Dutch-Indonesian relations could go "so wrong".

The ceremony was not the same for everyone. One widow, 93-year-old Anti Rukiyah, told AFP she was relieved to receive an apology. "At the same time, it happened so long ago, it doesn't matter anymore," she said, according to one report. Another widow, 92-year-old Wanti Binti Dodo, had not known the verdict was coming. "I can't believe it," she said. "I am happy, maybe I will get some money," AP reports.

The sources do not agree on who was paid, or how much. UCA News reports that Zegveld said each relative would receive €20,000, about US$27,000. The Jakarta Post gives the same amount. One report says the Dutch side had committed US$1.13 million for the community before the judgment, with a further US$242,000 for the plaintiffs or their families to follow. Al Jazeera reported in 2011 that the Dutch government had decided in 2009 to donate US$1.16 million to Balongsari, but had avoided the word "compensation". De Volkskrant, quoted by Al Jazeera, said it had lost track of the money once it was paid to Indonesian authorities.

The number of plaintiffs differs too. DutchNews and DW describe seven widows, one survivor and a daughter of another widow in the court case. Al Jazeera and JURIST describe seven widows and a survivor, and JURIST says the daughter's claim was barred by the time limit. One report counts eight widows and a survivor. The Dutch press release describes nine surviving relatives. The sources also report deaths during the case. One English-language report says the survivor Saih Bin Sakam died in May at the age of 88, and that two of the widows had died since the case began. AP reports one widow and one wounded man had died earlier that year.

The Dutch government also apologised to families of men executed in South Sulawesi in 1946 and 1947, in September 2013, according to DW. In March 2016 Foreign Minister Bert Koenders visited the memorial at Balongsari during an official visit to Jakarta. He said: "The deployment of military force in 1947 put the Netherlands on the wrong side of history." DW reports that he also said the Dutch government had apologised and that he hoped this would help reconciliation.

Some questions remain open. No soldier was prosecuted, and the 1948 finding was never followed by a trial. The court case was narrow, and the lawyer said it was unclear whether it would open the way to claims from other relatives of people killed in the wider war. The disagreement over the death toll has not been settled: the official 150 and the victims' group's 431 are still quoted side by side. For the people of Balongsari, the memorial and the apology are the public record of what happened on 9 December 1947.
